text.p: These are significant stories in the Nigerian press on Thursday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- Calm returns to oil town of Warri in the midwest after soldiers move in to seperate warring youths feuding over the relocation of the local council headquarters.
- Afrobeat music superstar Fela Anikulapo-Kuti granted bail by tribunal hearing charges against him for alleged possession and use of cannabis.
- Nigeria may lose about 295 million naira from the strike at Bonny terminal which stopped export of crude oil there for two days this week, oil industry sources said.
- New laws bar Nigerian trade unions from affiliating with foreign counterparts.

- Statistics rolled out by Lagos police say car theft in the sprawling metropolis has dropped to 11 in February 1997 from 300 in the same month a year ago and attributes this to "operation sweep" launched late year to combat crime.
- Federal government warns that it will not condone attacks on oil installations under guise of political agitations.

- A workshop by the organised private sector recommends that the government should set aside five years for the deregulation of all state monopolies such as the electricity, telecommunications and railways corporations.
- Shell oil company resumes exporting Bonny crude oil after a strike by workers of a contracting company is ended.
- Chief Ernest Shonekan, the chairman of "Vision 2010" committee planning Nigeria's future, urges the private sector to brace up for eventual privatisation of state enterprises.
- Nigerian human rights groups petition Swiss embassy in Lagos over maltreatment of their member by Geneva police.
- Shell votes $1.6 million to repair airports in Warri and Port Harcourt where it has big operations.
